messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: PromptScaffold is a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through four template slots (role, task, examples, output format) to write LLM prompts. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 students, template prompts scored higher on an automatic task score (0.74 vs 0.61) and raised self-rated confidence (4.1 vs 3.4), at the cost of slightly more time (7.5 vs 6.2 minutes).

sections.title: What the editor does
sections.text: The authors describe four slots: the role slot states who the model should act as, the task slot describes what to do, the examples slot asks for one to three input-output pairs, and the output format slot specifies the answer structure. Each slot has a short hint and example, and the editor assembles them into a prompt that users can preview and edit.

sections.title: How the study was run and what it found
sections.text: Participants completed three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, topic labelling, news summarisation) in both a free-form condition and the template condition, with one LLM and an automatic task score. The template improved the mean score, with the largest gain on topic labelling, and participants reported higher confidence. PaperLens's description of Table 1 shows the per-task figures, and the caption gives the design summary.

sections.title: Limits the authors name
sections.text: The authors note a small, homogeneous sample of university students, a single 70-minute session, three predefined tasks, one LLM, and reliance on automatic scores and self-reported confidence. They also report that several participants filled the slots mechanically, so the template's benefits may depend on how the purpose of each slot is explained.

PromptScaffold: Helping Non-Expert Users Write LLM Prompts with Structured Templates Mira Castellan, Joon-ho Reyes and Priya Valcourt School of Computing, Halden University of Technology Abstract. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience.
